questions.stem: Police believe Jordan may have committed a burglary and want to question him, but he has not been charged. Jordan is best described as a:
options: accused
witness
suspect
offender
questions.explanation: A suspect is a person police believe may have committed an offence but who has not yet been charged. Once charged, the person becomes the accused. An offender is a person who has been found guilty, and a witness is someone who saw or knows something relevant.

questions.stem: Mia has been charged with assault occasioning bodily harm and is awaiting trial. Which term correctly describes her and the conduct?
options: She is the suspect, because no court has yet found her guilty
She is the defendant in a civil action brought by the victim
She is the accused, and the assault is alleged until it is proved
She is the offender, because a charge is proof that she committed it
questions.explanation: After a charge is laid the person is the accused, and the offence remains alleged until it is proved beyond reasonable doubt or the person pleads guilty. Calling her an offender would ignore the presumption of innocence; a suspect has not yet been charged.

questions.stem: A person who suffers harm as a direct result of an offence is the:
options: witness
accused
informant
victim
questions.explanation: The victim is the person harmed by the offence. A witness gives evidence of what they saw, heard or know, and a victim may also be a witness. The accused is the person charged.

questions.stem: Under section 3 of the Criminal Code (Qld), crimes and misdemeanours are:
options: simple offences, which must always be decided by a magistrate sitting without a jury
regulatory offences, which can only be dealt with by an infringement notice
civil wrongs, for which the victim may sue to recover damages for any loss
indictable offences, which unless otherwise stated are prosecuted on indictment
questions.explanation: Section 3 divides offences into criminal and regulatory offences. Criminal offences are crimes, misdemeanours and simple offences. Crimes and misdemeanours are indictable, so unless otherwise expressly stated they are prosecuted on indictment; regulatory and simple offences may be dealt with summarily by a Magistrates Court.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts summary and indictable offences in Queensland?
options: Summary offences are Commonwealth offences tried in federal courts; indictable offences are offences against the Criminal Code made by Queensland
Summary offences are less serious and are decided by a magistrate; indictable offences are more serious and may be tried by judge and jury
Summary offences are more serious and are decided by a jury; indictable offences are less serious and are decided by a magistrate
Summary offences are civil wrongs decided in QCAT; indictable offences are criminal offences decided in the Magistrates Court
questions.explanation: Summary offences, such as public nuisance, are minor and are heard and decided by a magistrate. Indictable offences are more serious and, unless dealt with summarily, are tried in the District or Supreme Court before a judge and jury.

questions.stem: Why do Queensland laws allow many indictable offences to be dealt with summarily in the Magistrates Court?
options: It allows magistrates to impose higher penalties than District Court judges for the same offence
It removes the need for the prosecution to prove the offence beyond reasonable doubt
It ensures that every indictable offence is decided by a jury of twelve randomly chosen citizens
It saves time and cost for less serious examples of offences that would otherwise need a trial
questions.explanation: Dealing with less serious indictable offences summarily is quicker and cheaper for the courts and the parties than a trial on indictment. The standard of proof does not change, and summary hearings are decided by a magistrate, not a jury.

questions.stem: Assault occasioning bodily harm is best classified as an offence:
options: against the public interest
against the administration of justice
against the person
against property
questions.explanation: Offences against the person, such as assault, grievous bodily harm and murder, involve harm or threatened harm to a human being. Stealing, burglary and wilful damage are property offences.

questions.stem: Spray-painting graffiti on a railway bridge is most likely to be charged as wilful damage under section 469 of the Criminal Code (Qld). This is an offence:
options: against the public order
against the state
against property
against the person
questions.explanation: Wilful damage involves wilfully and unlawfully destroying or damaging property, so it is a property offence. Stealing and burglary are other examples of offences relating to property.

questions.stem: Which offence is best classified as an offence against the public interest or public order rather than against a particular person or property?
options: Public nuisance under the Summary Offences Act 2005 (Qld)
Stealing under section 398 of the Criminal Code (Qld)
Grievous bodily harm under section 320 of the Criminal Code (Qld)
Burglary under section 419 of the Criminal Code (Qld)
questions.explanation: Public nuisance involves behaviour, such as disorderly or offensive conduct, that interferes with the public's peaceful use of a place, so it is a public order offence. Stealing and burglary are property offences, and grievous bodily harm is an offence against the person.

questions.stem: Under section 245 of the Criminal Code (Qld), a person may commit an assault by:
options: refusing to stop and help another person who has been injured in a car accident on a highway
threatening to apply force, with an actual or apparent present ability to carry out the threat
insulting another person in a text message sent while they are in another state
accidentally bumping into another person while getting off a crowded train carriage at a station
questions.explanation: Section 245 defines assault to include striking, touching, moving or applying force to another person without consent, and attempting or threatening to apply force where the person has an actual or apparent present ability to carry it out. An insult with no threat of force is not an assault.

questions.stem: Under section 391 of the Criminal Code (Qld), a person steals if they:
options: accidentally damage another person's property while using it with their full knowledge and consent
fraudulently take, or fraudulently convert to their own use, anything capable of being stolen
borrow another person's property with permission and return it later than agreed
find property in a public place and hand it in to the nearest police station on the same day
questions.explanation: Stealing is defined in section 391 as fraudulently taking or converting anything capable of being stolen. 'Fraudulently' includes taking with an intent to permanently deprive the owner. Stealing is punished under section 398. Borrowing with permission or handing property in shows no fraudulent intent.

questions.stem: Ruby takes a phone from a cafe table, puts it in her pocket and walks out. She later says she meant to keep it. In proving stealing, the prosecution must show both:
options: that Ruby had stolen before and that the owner reported the theft to police at once
the taking of the phone and an intent to deprive the owner of it permanently
that the phone was worth more than $1,000 and that Ruby was seen leaving
that Ruby used force on the owner and that she sold the phone afterwards
questions.explanation: Stealing requires an act (fraudulently taking or converting the property) and the necessary state of mind, such as an intent to permanently deprive the owner. Value, force, previous offending and the timing of a report are not elements of stealing; force would make it robbery.

questions.stem: In criminal law, the actus reus of wilful damage would be:
options: the cost of repairing the property that was damaged
the physical act of damaging another person's property
the accused's intention to damage another person's property
the police officer's reasonable suspicion that damage occurred
questions.explanation: The actus reus is the physical element, the act or omission itself, here damaging the property. The intention is part of the mens rea, the mental element. The cost of repair may affect the penalty but is not the actus reus.

questions.stem: Which correctly matches each Criminal Code (Qld) offence with its maximum penalty?
options: Common assault: 1 year; grievous bodily harm: 7 years
Common assault: 3 years; grievous bodily harm: 14 years
Common assault: 14 years; grievous bodily harm: 3 years
Common assault: 7 years; grievous bodily harm: life
questions.explanation: Common assault under section 335 has a maximum of 3 years' imprisonment, assault occasioning bodily harm under section 339 a maximum of 7 years, and grievous bodily harm under section 320 a maximum of 14 years. Higher maximums apply where circumstances of aggravation exist.

questions.stem: Leo punches Sam once, splitting his lip, which needs stitches but heals completely. Under the Criminal Code (Qld), which charge best fits?
options: Grievous bodily harm, because any injury needing medical treatment is grievous
Common assault only, because the injury healed completely within a few weeks
Wilful damage, because Sam's body was damaged by a deliberate act
Assault occasioning bodily harm, because the injury interferes with health or comfort
questions.explanation: Bodily harm is any bodily injury that interferes with health or comfort, so a split lip needing stitches fits assault occasioning bodily harm. Grievous bodily harm requires a more serious injury, such as the loss of a distinct part or organ of the body, serious disfigurement, or an injury that if left untreated would be likely to endanger life or cause permanent injury to health.

questions.stem: Under section 365 of the Police Powers and Responsibilities Act 2000 (Qld), a police officer may arrest a person without a warrant if the officer reasonably suspects the person has committed an offence and:
options: it is reasonably necessary for a listed reason, such as preventing the offence continuing
the person refuses to answer the officer's questions about where they have been
a member of the public asks the officer to arrest the person straight away at the scene
the officer has already arrested the same person on an earlier occasion for a different offence
questions.explanation: Section 365 requires both a reasonable suspicion and that the arrest is reasonably necessary for a listed reason, such as preventing the offence continuing, establishing identity, ensuring court attendance, preserving evidence or protecting a person's safety. Refusing to answer questions is an exercise of the right to silence.

questions.stem: Instead of arresting a person for a minor offence, a Queensland police officer may issue a notice to appear. This document:
options: orders the person to stay in police custody until the court hearing
requires the person to attend court on a set date to answer the charge
allows police to search the person's home without a search warrant
records that the person has already been found guilty by a magistrate
questions.explanation: A notice to appear under section 382 is a way of starting a proceeding without taking the person into custody; it requires them to attend court on a stated date. It avoids the intrusion of arrest for minor matters, which reflects arrest being used only where necessary.

questions.stem: A summons is:
options: a formal warning given to a child by police instead of starting a proceeding
a court document requiring a person to attend court to answer a complaint
a police power to detain a person for questioning for up to eight hours
a written order allowing police to enter and search a named place
questions.explanation: A complaint and summons is another way to start a prosecution without arrest: a court document requires the defendant to attend court on a stated date. A written order allowing entry and search is a search warrant, and a formal warning to a child is a caution.

questions.stem: To obtain a search warrant under the Police Powers and Responsibilities Act 2000 (Qld), police usually apply to a justice of the peace, who must be satisfied that:
options: the occupier of the place has previously been convicted of a similar offence in Queensland
the occupier has refused to answer police questions about the offence
a senior police officer has approved the search in writing beforehand
there are reasonable grounds for suspecting evidence of an offence is, or soon will be, at the place
questions.explanation: Under sections 150 and 151, the issuer must be satisfied there are reasonable grounds for suspecting evidence is at the place or will be within the next 72 hours. Requiring an independent person to approve the search protects privacy from arbitrary police entry.

questions.stem: Why does the law require police to obtain a warrant from an independent issuer before searching a home in most cases?
options: It allows the occupier of the home to choose which rooms police may search and which rooms they may not
It provides an independent check on police power, balancing privacy with the need to investigate crime
It makes it impossible for police to search any home in which an offence is believed to have occurred
It ensures that the occupier is told about the search several days before it takes place
questions.explanation: A warrant requires an independent justice of the peace, magistrate or judge to be satisfied that reasonable grounds exist, so police cannot enter homes on a whim. It balances the individual's right to privacy with society's need for evidence to be gathered. Warrants are not announced days in advance.

questions.stem: Under section 403 of the Police Powers and Responsibilities Act 2000 (Qld), an arrested person suspected of an indictable offence may be detained for questioning for a reasonable time of not more than:
options: 8 hours, of which no more than 4 hours may be questioning
24 hours, of which no more than 12 hours may be questioning
4 hours, of which no more than 2 hours may be questioning
48 hours, with no limit on how long questioning may last
questions.explanation: The detention period is a reasonable time of up to 8 hours, and questioning within it may not exceed 4 hours; time out, for example to contact a lawyer, is not counted. Police may apply to a magistrate, or in some cases a justice of the peace, to extend the period.

questions.stem: Police want to hold a suspect beyond the detention period to finish questioning about a serious offence. Which statement is correct?
options: They must apply for an extension, and the magistrate must be satisfied further detention is necessary
They may keep questioning for as long as needed, because the offence is serious
They must release the suspect and can never question them again about the offence
They may extend the period themselves if a senior officer agrees in writing that it is necessary
questions.explanation: Under sections 405 and 406, an extension must be sought from a magistrate or, in some cases, a justice of the peace, who must be satisfied that further detention is necessary, for example to preserve evidence or complete questioning, and that the investigation is being conducted properly and without delay.

questions.stem: Before questioning a person suspected of an indictable offence, police must tell them that they may contact a lawyer and give them a reasonable opportunity to do so. This requirement mainly:
options: allows police to keep the suspect in custody for longer than the law allows
requires the lawyer to answer police questions on the suspect's behalf
means the suspect must give a full account of events to the lawyer and police
helps suspects understand and exercise their rights while in custody
questions.explanation: Section 418 requires police to inform a suspect of an indictable offence of the right to speak with a lawyer, and a friend or relative, before questioning. Legal advice helps the suspect understand their rights, including the right to silence, which supports just outcomes.

questions.stem: Before questioning a person about an indictable offence, Queensland police must caution them. The caution tells the person that:
options: they must answer every question, or they will be charged with obstructing police
they will receive a lighter sentence if they confess to the offence straight away
their silence will be treated by the court as evidence that they are guilty
they do not have to say anything, and anything they say may be used as evidence
questions.explanation: Under section 431, police must caution the person that they need not say anything and that anything they say may later be used in evidence. The right to silence means silence during questioning cannot generally be used as evidence of guilt.

questions.stem: A suspect in police custody refuses to answer questions about a robbery but gives his correct name and address when lawfully required. Which statement is correct?
options: He has broken the law, because a suspect in custody must answer every question that police ask about the offence
He has waived his right to silence completely by giving police his name and address
He must now give evidence at his trial, because he refused to answer police questions
He is exercising his right to silence, which does not extend to refusing to give his name and address when lawfully required
questions.explanation: The right to silence lets a suspect decline to answer questions about the offence, and silence generally cannot be used to suggest guilt. However, police may require a person to state their name and address in prescribed circumstances, and failing to do so can be an offence. Giving these details does not waive the right to silence.

questions.stem: Police record the interview with a suspect electronically. Which is the main reason this protects both the suspect and police?
options: It means the suspect no longer has the right to remain silent during the interview
It replaces the need for police to caution the suspect before questioning begins
It provides an accurate record of what was said, reducing disputes about admissions
It allows the court to convict without hearing any other evidence about the offence
questions.explanation: An electronic record shows exactly what was asked and answered, and how, which helps the court decide whether admissions were made voluntarily and protects police against false claims of misconduct. The suspect keeps the right to silence, and the caution must still be given.

questions.stem: A police officer stops a group of teenagers in a park and decides to give them a warning rather than charging one with public nuisance. Which statement best evaluates this use of police discretion?
options: It guarantees equal treatment, because every officer will make exactly the same decision in every case
It is unlawful, because only a magistrate can decide not to proceed with a charge against a person
It can keep minor offenders out of court, but inconsistent use may treat similar people differently
It is unlawful, because police must charge every person they suspect of an offence
questions.explanation: Police discretion allows officers to respond in proportion to the conduct, saving court resources and avoiding the harm of a criminal record for minor matters. However, discretion can be applied inconsistently or with bias, which raises concerns about equality before the law.

questions.stem: Fingerprints and DNA collected at a crime scene are examples of:
options: documentary evidence
character evidence
forensic (physical) evidence
witness testimony
questions.explanation: Forensic evidence is physical material analysed scientifically, such as fingerprints, DNA, fibres and blood. Testimony is what a witness says in court, documentary evidence includes records and documents, and character evidence relates to a person's reputation.

questions.stem: After a person is arrested, the Police Powers and Responsibilities Act 2000 (Qld) allows police to take identifying particulars. These include:
options: statements from the person's employer
photographs, fingerprints and palm prints
medical records held by the person's doctor
the person's bank records and tax returns
questions.explanation: Under section 467, police may generally take identifying particulars of a person in custody for an offence, which include photographs, fingerprints, palm prints, footprints, voiceprints and handwriting. Medical, bank and employment records would require other legal processes.

questions.stem: Eli's fingerprints and DNA sample were taken after he was charged with burglary. He is later acquitted and has no other relevant charges. What does Queensland law generally require?
options: Police may keep them permanently in case he offends in the future
They must be given to Eli to keep as evidence of his acquittal
They must be sent to a national database for use by all police services
The particulars and DNA must be destroyed within a reasonable time
questions.explanation: If a person is found not guilty or the charge is withdrawn, identifying particulars and DNA samples must generally be destroyed within a reasonable time, unless the person is suspected of, charged with or found guilty of another relevant offence. This protects the privacy of people the law presumes innocent.

questions.stem: Which argument best supports keeping DNA profiles on a database only for people convicted of offences?
options: It means police will no longer need to collect DNA at crime scenes at all
It stops courts from using DNA evidence against people charged with offences
It protects the privacy of people who are presumed innocent, while still helping solve future crimes
It ensures that no crime involving DNA evidence can ever go unsolved by police anywhere in Queensland
questions.explanation: Limiting retention to convicted people balances the investigative value of a DNA database with the privacy and presumption of innocence of people who were never found guilty. No database can guarantee every crime is solved, and DNA remains usable evidence at trial.

questions.stem: Commonwealth law requires telecommunications providers to keep certain metadata about their customers' communications for at least two years. Metadata includes:
options: the full text of every email and text message that is sent
the passwords that customers use for their online accounts
the time, date and parties to a call, but not what was said
the full recorded content of every phone call that is made
questions.explanation: Metadata is information about a communication, such as who it was between, when and for how long, but not its content. The data retention scheme in the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 (Cth) requires providers to retain it for two years. Accessing content generally requires an interception warrant.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the retention of metadata in balancing individual rights with society's need for order?
options: It is fully justified, because it lets police read the content of all messages and emails without any warrant
It is ineffective, because criminals never use mobile phones or the internet in planning offences
It helps police investigate serious crime, but storing everyone's data affects the privacy of people never suspected of anything
It has no effect on privacy, because metadata reveals nothing about a person's activities or contacts
questions.explanation: Metadata can reveal patterns of contact and location that help solve crime, which supports society's need for order. However, it is collected about everyone, not just suspects, and can reveal a great deal about a person's life, which raises privacy concerns. Metadata does not include message content.

questions.stem: Under section 29 of the Criminal Code (Qld), a person is not criminally responsible for any act or omission if they are under the age of:
options: 10 years
12 years
14 years
8 years
questions.explanation: Section 29(1) sets the minimum age of criminal responsibility at 10. Under section 29(2), a child under 14 is not criminally responsible unless it is proved that they had capacity to know they ought not to do the act.

questions.stem: Police want to question a 15-year-old about a stolen car. Which safeguard does the Police Powers and Responsibilities Act 2000 (Qld) generally require?
options: The questioning must take place in the Childrens Court before a magistrate
The child must answer all questions because the right to silence applies only to adults
A support person, such as a parent or lawyer, must be present during questioning
The child must first be found guilty before police may ask any questions
questions.explanation: Section 421 provides extra safeguards for children, including the presence of a support person during questioning. This addresses the imbalance of power between a young person and police. Children have the same right to silence as adults.

questions.stem: A Queensland government proposes giving police wider powers to search and detain young people in areas with high youth crime. Which response best weighs both sides of the issue?
options: Wider powers have no effect on rights, because children are not given any protection by police powers laws
Wider powers may reduce offending, but they risk breaching children's rights and harming their contact with police
Wider powers will end youth crime, because young people never offend where police are present
Wider powers are unlawful, because the Queensland Parliament cannot make laws about children
questions.explanation: Youth justice debates weigh community safety against the rights and wellbeing of children, who are more vulnerable in dealing with police. Wider powers may deter offending, but they can also lead to over-policing and early contact with the justice system, which is linked to further offending.

questions.stem: Under Queensland's Charter of Victims' Rights, a victim of a violent crime is generally entitled to be:
options: paid compensation by the police before any person is charged with the offence
kept informed about the progress of the police investigation, unless this could jeopardise it
given the power to decide whether the police will charge the suspect with an offence
told the identity of every witness who has made a statement to police about the crime
questions.explanation: The Charter requires agencies to keep victims informed of the progress of the investigation, unless this may jeopardise it, and to tell them of major decisions such as charges laid. Decisions to charge rest with police and prosecutors, not victims.

questions.stem: A student is analysing trends in crimes reported to police in Queensland over ten years. Which sources are most appropriate?
options: Television crime dramas set in Brisbane and other Queensland cities
Queensland Police Service crime statistics and the Queensland Government Statistician's Office
Newspaper headlines about crime and comments posted on social media
A survey of the student's classmates about crimes they have heard of in their suburbs
questions.explanation: Official recorded crime data from the Queensland Police Service and analysis by the Queensland Government Statistician's Office are reliable and consistent over time. The ABS also publishes national recorded crime data. Media coverage and anecdotes are not representative of crime levels.

questions.stem: Recorded crime figures may underestimate the true level of crime. Which is the main reason?
options: Crimes committed by children are never counted in official crime statistics at all
Many offences, such as some assaults and sexual offences, are never reported to police
Police record every offence twice, so the official figures always have to be halved
Only offences that lead to a conviction are included in recorded crime data
questions.explanation: Recorded crime includes only offences that come to police attention. Unreported crime, sometimes called the 'dark figure' of crime, is why surveys of victims are used alongside police data. Recorded crime counts offences reported or detected, not only those leading to convictions.

questions.stem: Recorded drug offences in a Queensland region rise sharply in the year police run a targeted drug operation. Which is the best interpretation?
options: The rise may reflect increased police detection rather than more drug use
The rise proves that drug use doubled in the region during that year
The rise shows that the operation caused people to start using drugs
The rise means the figures for that year must be inaccurate and should be ignored
questions.explanation: Drug offences are mostly detected by police rather than reported by victims, so recorded numbers depend heavily on police activity. A targeted operation increases detection, so a rise may not mean more offending. Analysing crime data means considering how it was collected.
